Fractures of the Navicular Bone
 CORE
July 31, 2026
Jesse Forbes Doty, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the local anatomy and arterial supply of the navicular bone.
Recognize common navicular bone mechanisms of injury and fracture patterns.
Become familiar with physical examination findings and imaging studies diagnostic of
navicular bone fractures.
Implement appropriate treatment options for the management of specific navicular bone
fracture types.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of the tarsal navicular bone may result from a single traumatic event or chronic
overload. The navicular bone also is susceptible to osteonecrosis because of its complex anatomy

and unique blood supply1 (Resource 1). Although the navicular is injured less often than the talus
or calcaneus, it is the most commonly injured lesser tarsal bone2 (Resource 2).
Epidemiology
Chronic overuse
Altered vascularity
Altered foot mechanics
Low-energy twisting injuries to the midfoot
High-energy axial forces

Epidemiology
Navicular stress fractures, which are observed most commonly in running athletes, may
be to the result of chronic overuse, altered vascularity, or altered foot mechanics, such
as cavus foot3 (Resource 3). Navicular avulsion fractures are caused by low-energy
twisting injuries to the midfoot,1 whereas navicular body fractures often result from
high-energy axial forces, such as a motor vehicle collision or a fall from a height.2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology of the Navicular Bone
Saddle-shaped bone
Articulates distally with the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones
Articulates proximally with the talus bone
Smaller lateral articulations are positioned between the calcaneus and cuboid bones.
The medial tuberosity serves as the primary insertion of the posterior tibial tendon.
The plantar rim attaches to the fibrocartilaginous spring ligament.
The talonavicular articulation maintains a swivel-like motion.

Osteology of the Navicular Bone

AAOS | Fractures of the Navicular Bone
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000646
2/18

The navicular is a saddle-shaped bone that articulates distally with the medial,
intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones and proximally with the talus. It also has
smaller lateral articulations with the calcaneus and cuboid bones. The medial tuberosity
serves as the attachment point for the posterior tibial tendon, and the plantar rim serves
as the attachment point of the fibrocartilaginous spring ligament.
The talonavicular articulation, an essential joint of the foot, is critical in maintaining
swivel motion at the junction of the hindfoot and midfoot. During ambulation, motion
occurs with inversion and eversion. The talonavicular articulation also is linked to
mobility at the subtalar and calcaneocuboid joints, and an injury at any of these
junctions has major effects on the mechanics of the remaining joints. Similarly, fusion of
any of these joints limits mobility of the remaining nonfused joints. Eversion of the
subtalar joint during heel strike unlocks and permits motion through the talonavicular
joint, allowing the midfoot to settle and dampen the ground reaction force during
ambulation. Inversion of the subtalar joint during push-off rigidifies the talonavicular
joint so it acts as a lever arm during ambulation. This often is referred to as the
transverse tarsal mechanism.2
The navicular bone forms the uppermost position of the medial longitudinal arch and,
therefore, serves as the keystone for vertical stress.2
Very little motion occurs through the naviculocuneiform joints, which occasionally are
considered nonessential joints.
Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply to the navicular bone is reportedly limited in the central watershed portion.
Dense intraosseous blood supply
The dorsal branches of the dorsalis pedis artery serve the dorsal and lateral aspects of the
navicular bone.
The medial plantar branches of the posterior tibial artery serve the plantarmedial portion of
the bone.


Vascular Anatomy
Historically, the blood supply to the navicular bone was considered limited in its central
watershed portion, making this area susceptible to fractures; however, vascular studies
have shown a dense intraosseous blood supply throughout the bone in most individuals,
suggesting that only a small group of individuals are at risk of navicular stress fractures
based on vascularity. If a true zone of hypovascularity is identified, it often is located
within the central dorsal third of the bone. In general, the dorsomedial branches of the
dorsalis pedis artery serve the dorsal and lateral aspects of the navicular bone, whereas
the medial plantar branches of the posterior tibial artery serve the plantarmedial
portion4 (Resource 4).
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Avulsion Fractures
Avulsion fractures account for one-half of all navicular fractures.
Medial avulsion results from stress imposed by the tibialis posterior muscle.
Plantar avulsion results from stress imposed by the spring ligament.

Avulsion Fractures
Avulsion injuries constitute approximately one-half of all navicular fractures. Avulsion of
the dorsal lip results from stress imposed by the deltoid ligament during eversion of the
foot. Medial avulsion results from stress imposed by the tibialis posterior muscle. Finally,
plantar avulsion results from stress imposed by the spring ligament5 (Resource 5).
Fractures of the Tuberosity
Foot eversion and contraction of the posterior tibial tendon results in diastasis.

Fractures of the Tuberosity
The principal mechanism in fracture of the tuberosity of the navicular bone is eversion
and contraction of the posterior tibial tendon, which may cause diastasis of a preexisting
accessory navicular bone.
Fractures of the Navicular Body (Figure 1)

Figure 1 Illustrations of navicular fractures. A, Lateral view shows a type I navicular fracture (axial
plane fracture line). B, AP view shows a type II navicular fracture (sagittal plane fracture line). The
arrows indicate the direction of applied force. Note the subluxation of the talonavicular joint and
proximal migration of the first ray, a common component of type II fractures. C, AP view shows a
type III navicular fracture. Note the comminution, displacement, and incongruity of the
talonavicular and naviculocuneiform joints. The arrow indicates the direction of applied force.
(Reproduced from Stroud CC: Fractures of the midtarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges, in
Richardson EG, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2003, p 57-67.)
Axial loading
Motor vehicle collisions or a fall from height
Dual approach for comminuted fractures
In patients with a fracture of the navicular body, the mechanism of injury is axial loading. These
injuries often involve high-energy mechanisms, such as a motor vehicle collision or a fall from
height. Given the displacement, comminution, soft-tissue injury, and tenuous blood supply
associated with fractures of the navicular body, the surgeon faces several technical challenges in
attempting to restore function.2
Stress Fractures
Common in runners
Represent 15% to 35% of all foot and ankle stress fractures
Considered high risk for nonunion
Foot strike creates stress primarily at the central third of the navicular bone.

Stress Fractures
Navicular stress fractures, which represent 15% to 35% of all foot and ankle stress
fractures, commonly affect running athletes. If acute, these injuries may be managed
nonsurgically or surgically, depending on the patient’s activity level. Similar to stress
fractures of the anterior tibial shaft, medial malleolus, and fifth metatarsal, navicular
stress fractures are considered high risk for delayed healing. Vascularity and
biomechanics are the primary causes of delayed healing.3 Some evidence suggests a
zone of hypovascularity is present at the central dorsal third of the bone.4 During foot

strike, forces are transferred to the navicular from the medial and intermediate
cuneiform. Medially, these forces are transitioned proximally to the talar head. Laterally,
these forces are not transitioned to the talar head, thereby creating a zone of shearing.
In addition, forces of the posterior tibial tendon create tension on the medial bone.
Therefore, the stress created by these coupled forces is centered primarily at the central
third of the navicular bone3,6 (Resource 6).
Injury Classification
The Sangeorzan system classifies navicular fractures based on fracture lines and the degree of
comminution.
Stress fractures are referred to as acute or chronic.

Injury Classification
The Sangeorzan classification of fractures of the navicular body is based on the plane of
the fracture lines and the degree of comminution. Type I fractures are transverse, with a
dorsal fragment comprising less than 50% of the bone; they are not associated with a
foot deformity. Type II fractures are oblique from dorsolateral to plantarmedial and may
be associated with forefoot adduction. Type III fractures generally are comminuted
centrally or laterally and may be associated with forefoot abduction or calcaneus and
cuboid fractures.1 Stress fractures often are referred to as acute or chronic.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Pain or tenderness radiating along the medial arch
Pain may be relieved by rest and exacerbated by impact activity.
Tenderness to palpation at the dorsoproximal portion of the central third of the bone


Patient History and Physical Examination
Clinically, patients with a navicular fracture report dorsomedial foot pain radiating along
the medial arch. Gentle palpation of the medial column produces tenderness. In patients
with a high-energy, acute fracture, physicians should maintain a low threshold for
evaluation of associated lower extremity injuries. With a stress fracture, the pain may be
relieved with rest and exacerbated with impact activity. Tenderness to palpation often is
detected at the dorsoproximal portion of the central third of the bone, typically between
the anterior tibial and extensor hallucis tendons.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Obtained for acute and chronic injuries
Radiographic changes may lag behind symptoms for weeks.
Three-view foot series: AP, lateral, and internal oblique

Radiography
If a navicular injury is clinically suspected, radiographs should be obtained early for
acute and chronic injuries. In the work up of stress fractures, radiographic changes may
lag behind symptoms for weeks. A standard, plain, three-view radiographic foot series
(ie, AP, lateral, and internal oblique views) should be obtained. For tuberosity avulsions,
external oblique radiographs may be useful.1
Computed Tomography
Useful for characterizing the fracture pattern and determining management
May help determine surgical approach and type of internal fixation
Helpful in diagnosing stress fractures


Computed Tomography
CT is useful for characterizing the navicular fracture pattern. In acute traumatic injuries,
this information may inform the surgical approach and determine the optimal type and
application of internal fixation.1 In stress fractures, CT may facilitate diagnosis, depict the
stage of fracture healing, and indicate if surgical or nonsurgical management is
indicated.3 Most importantly, CT can definitively identify fracture displacement, which
also affects management.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Ordered early in the evaluation for navicular stress fractures
Reveals the extent of the fracture and marrow edema
Not useful for the work up of high-energy body fractures
Helpful in diagnosing or assessing low-injury avulsion fractures

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI generally is performed early in the evaluation of navicular stress fractures to
confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the extent of the fracture and marrow edema.3
Although MRI is not useful in the work up of high-energy body fractures, it may be
helpful in diagnosing or determining associated injuries in low-injury avulsion fractures.3
Bone Scintigraphy
Most sensitive for diagnosis if MRI is contraindicated or findings are equivocal.
Not as useful in evaluating an acute navicular injury

Bone Scintigraphy

If MRI is contraindicated (eg, in patients with a cardiac pacemaker) or results are
equivocal in the work up of navicular stress fractures, then bone scintigraphy is the most
sensitive alternative imaging modality for diagnosis; however, bone scintigraphy is less
useful in evaluating acute injuries.3
Management: Varies by Fracture Type
Avulsion Fractures
Immediate management consists of immobilization.
Surgical management may be indicated for fragments involving more than 25% of the articular
surface.

Avulsion Fractures
Acute management consists of immobilization with delayed excision of chronically
painful fragments. Surgical reduction and fixation may be best for fractures with
fragments involving more than 25% of the articular surface.5
Tuberosity Fractures
Most can be managed via immobilization.
Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is indicated in patients with more than 5 mm of
diastasis or patients with large intra-articular fracture fragments.
Nonunion may be managed via late excision and reattachment of the posterior tibial tendon.

Tuberosity Fractures
Most avulsion fractures of the tuberosity can be managed via immobilization. Acute ORIF
may be indicated in patients with an acute injury and more than 5 mm of diastasis and

patients with intra-articular fracture fragments. Symptomatic nonunion is managed via
late excision and reattachment of the posterior tibial tendon.1
Body Fractures
Nondisplaced type I and II navicular body fractures often are managed nonsurgically.
With displaced type I and type II fractures, medial incision may allow for use of independent
lag screws to preserve tenuous blood supply.
Type IV fractures require ORIF.
A plate or external fixator may be used to maintain the length of the medial column.

Body Fractures
Nondisplaced type I and type II fractures often can be managed nonsurgically (ie, after
CT evaluation to assess fracture displacement). With displaced type I and type II fractures
or with disruption of the talonavicular joint, a medial incision generally is used. This
allows for the use of independent lag screws in the major bone fragments and is thought
to preserve the tenuous blood supply. Type III fractures require ORIF. In patients with
lateral comminution, a dual anteromedial and lateral approach may be used to restore
the articulation at the talonavicular joint and maintain the length of the medial column.
In some patients, a spanning external fixator or plate may help maintain the length of
the medial column of the foot after fixation of the primary fracture fragments.2
Stress Fractures
Early nonsurgical management of navicular stress fractures via immobilization and non‒weight
bearing may be successful.
Surgical management is recommended for navicular stress fractures in some patients.
A bone graft encourages healing.
Metabolic optimization of the patient is imperative.


Stress Fractures
Nonsurgical management of navicular stress fractures via cast or boot immobilization
and non‒weight bearing may be successful early in the treatment course. Surgical
management often is recommended for fractures that become chronically symptomatic,
are complete, have a medullary cyst, or exhibit nonunion. Bone grafting may promote
healing7 (Resource 7). Metabolic optimization of the patient also is imperative in the
management of navicular stress fractures.3
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
A CT scan is recommended for determining the surgical approach and technique.

Preoperative Planning
Appropriate imaging studies, including a three-view radiographic series of the foot, are
necessary. A CT scan is recommended to determine the most appropriate surgical
approach, select reduction techniques, plan the trajectory of screws, and anticipate plate
placement.
Patient Positioning
To access the medial column, the patient is placed in the supine position and externally
rotated.
To access the lateral column, the patient is placed in the sloppy lateral position (ie, supine with
a large bump).
For plantigrade positioning of the foot, a triangle may be used.


Patient Positioning
The patient generally is placed in the supine position with the foot externally rotated at
the end of the surgical table to access the medial column. The sloppy lateral position, or
a bump under the hip to roll the leg internally, may be beneficial if the lateral column
requires access. A triangle can be placed under the knee to allow for more plantigrade
positioning of the foot.
Surgical Approach
Direct dorsal approach used to excise or fixate dorsal fractures
Type 1 and type 2 fractures accessed via a medial approach
Dual medial and lateral approach often used for type III fractures

Surgical Approach
For excision or surgical fixation, dorsal avulsion fractures often are accessed via a direct
dorsal approach. This approach also may be useful for appropriate bone grafting of
stress fractures. Tuberosity avulsion and type I and type II navicular body fractures often
are accessed via a medial approach to allow for incorporation of the large fragment with
medial to lateral screw trajectories. A dual medial and lateral approach often is used in
comminuted type III fractures.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Screw fixation for large dorsal and tuberosity avulsion fractures
Screw compression provided for type I, type II, and stress fractures
Bridging external fixators or internal plates maintains the length and stability of the medial
column.


Surgical Fracture Fixation
Screw fixation often is useful for large dorsal avulsion and tuberosity avulsion fractures.
Screws also may provide excellent compression for the simple fracture lines observed in
type I, type II, and stress fractures. Mini-fragment plates may provide additional stability
in type III comminuted fractures. Some high-energy fractures may benefit from
temporary bridging of external fixators or internal plates to maintain the length and
stability of the medial column.2
In the navicular bone, screws traditionally traverse from lateral to medial because the
fracture line is most commonly observed in the lateral one-third of the bone. To achieve
the best compression without distortion, the angle of screw placement is ideally
perpendicular to the fracture line. Given that the fracture pattern is traditionally
dorsomedial to plantarlateral, placement of lateral-to-medial screws perpendicular to
the fracture line is difficult because of the cuboid. Placement of screws from
plantarlateral to dorsomedial also is difficult because the cuboid occupies this location
and because drilling in the normal plane is not possible. Therefore, these screws may be
compromised by their traditional placement dorsomedial to plantarmedial.
Postoperative Management
No weight bearing is imperative.
Cast immobilization in the immediate postoperative period
6 weeks of non‒weight bearing and 6 weeks of ambulation in a walking boot
To evaluate healing, CT may be useful postoperatively.

Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, a period of non-weight bearing is imperative; many surgeons
recommend cast immobilization in the immediate postoperative period. Most surgeons
recommend at least 6 weeks of non‒weight bearing followed by 6 weeks of ambulation
in a walking boot. Postoperative CT may help evaluate healing if necessary, particularly in

9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Navicular Bone
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000646
14/18

athletes attempting to return to sports activity. The fracture must heal sufficiently before
return to sports activity, and assessment of sufficient healing is better with CT than plain
radiographs.
Complications/Outcomes
Postoperative complications may include nonunion or malunion.
Osteonecrosis is commonly reported after type I and type IV navicular fractures.
In a study of 21 patients who were surgically treated for a displaced fracture of the tarsal
navicular, 67% had good results.

Complications/Outcomes
Nonunion or malunion with failure to anatomically reduce the articular surface may lead
to chronic pain and altered hindfoot mechanics8 (Resource 8). Traumatic osteonecrosis
is most commonly reported after type I and type III navicular body fractures. The blood
supply may have been disrupted at the time of high-energy trauma, with vascular injury
and periosteal stripping. This vascular insult may be further aggravated by surgical
dissection9 (Resource 9). Regardless, Sangeorzan et al10 reported that 67% of 21
patients with a navicular body fracture had good results at a mean follow-up of 44
months after surgical treatment, with six of the patients having some degree of
osteonecrosis. Most patients with partial osteonecrosis still had acceptable outcomes10
(Resource 10).
Mark as Complete
